title: THE RELATIONSHIP GOD NEVER APPROVED… BUT YOU STILL WON’T LET GO
paragraphs: THE RELATIONSHIP GOD NEVER APPROVED… BUT YOU STILL WON’T LET GO
When losing them feels unbearable, but keeping them may be costing you your obedience, your peace, and the version of you that Jesus is trying to restore.
There is a kind of relationship you rarely hear people confess about in church.
Not because it is rare.
Because it is embarrassing.
It is the relationship you keep defending even though, somewhere beneath all the excuses, you already know something is wrong.
You have prayed about it.
Cried about it.
Broken up and gone back.
Deleted the messages and restored them.
Blocked the number and unblocked it before the night was over.
You have called the confusion “complicated.”
You have called the attachment “love.”
You have called the repeated compromise “a season.”
You may have even called the relationship “God’s will” because admitting otherwise would force you to confront a terrifying possibility:
What if the person you are begging God to let you keep is connected to the very compromise God is asking you to surrender?
Read that again.
Because this is not an article about God cruelly taking people away from you.
This is about Jesus loving you too much to bless what is teaching your heart to live without wholehearted obedience to Him.
And before going further, something must be made clear.
Not every difficult relationship is a relationship God disapproves of.
Conflict does not automatically mean “God said leave.”
Disagreement does not prove someone is wrong for you.

A painful season is not necessarily divine permission to abandon a marriage covenant. Scripture treats marriage seriously, and situations involving abuse, coercion, threats, or danger require wise pastoral and professional help rather than simplistic internet slogans.
Nor should someone manipulate another person by declaring, “God told me you are not the one.”
This is not about superstition.
It is not about hunting for mystical signs.
It is about Scripture.
Fruit.
Holiness.
Truth.
Obedience.
And whether your relationship is helping you follow Jesus or repeatedly requiring you to negotiate with what He has already said.
Because sometimes the most dangerous relationship is not the one that obviously destroys you.
It is the one that slowly teaches you how to disobey God without feeling shocked anymore.
At first, you felt conviction.
Then you found explanations.
At first, crossing the boundary terrified you.
Eventually, you started moving the boundary.
At first, you prayed, “Lord, if this is not from You, remove it.”
Then the possibility of losing them became real.
And suddenly your prayer changed.
“Lord… please make this work.”
There is an uncomfortable difference between asking God for His will and asking God to approve ours.
Jesus Himself showed us what surrender sounds like.
In Gethsemane, facing suffering beyond what we can comprehend, He prayed:
“Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” — Luke 22:42
The Greek is devastatingly beautiful:
πλὴν μὴ τὸ θέλημά μου ἀλλὰ τὸ σὸν γινέσθω
plēn mē to thelēma mou alla to son ginesthō
The heart of it is unmistakable:
Not my will.
Yours.
That is surrender.
And surrender becomes painfully real when God’s will touches the person you desperately want to keep.
It is easy to sing, “Jesus, You are Lord,” when obedience costs nothing.
But what happens when following Christ threatens something your emotions have made sacred?
That is where lordship stops being vocabulary.
It becomes a cross.
Jesus said:
“If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me.” — Matthew 16:24
The Greek word translated “deny” is ἀπαρνησάσθω — aparnēsasthō.
It carries the force of denying or renouncing oneself.
Jesus was not calling His disciples into comfortable Christianity decorated with occasional sacrifice.
He was calling them into a life where He becomes greater than the self.
Greater than appetite.
Greater than approval.
Greater than romance.
Greater than loneliness.
Greater even than the person you thought you could never live without.
And maybe that is where this article found you.
You love them.
That is what makes this hurt.
Maybe there are beautiful memories.
Maybe they held you while you cried.
Maybe they know parts of you nobody else knows.
Maybe you have imagined marriage, children, anniversaries, a home, growing old together.
Maybe they are not even a terrible person.
But “not terrible” and “God-honoring” are not identical.
Someone can be charming and still pull you from Christ.
Someone can be generous and still reject the God you worship.
Someone can say “I love you” while repeatedly pressuring you toward what Scripture calls sin.
Someone can make your heart race while your spiritual life slowly suffocates.
And sometimes the warning is not that the person is monstrous.
It is that the relationship has become an altar.
You cannot imagine surrendering it.
You cannot imagine being okay without it.
You know what Scripture says, but their opinion has begun carrying more emotional authority than God’s Word.
That is when love can become idolatry.
God’s first commandment to Israel was uncompromising:
“You shall have no other gods before me.” — Exodus 20:3
The Hebrew reads:
לֹא יִהְיֶה־לְךָ אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים עַל־פָּנָי
Lo yihyeh-lekha elohim acherim al-panai.
No other gods before Me.
Most modern idols do not look like statues.
Sometimes an idol has a contact photo.
Sometimes you text it goodnight.
Sometimes you are terrified it will leave.
The question is not simply, “Do I love this person?”
The deeper question is:
Has keeping this person become more important to me than obeying Jesus?
That question can expose everything.
Because biblical love does not need rebellion against God in order to survive.
Scripture says:
“For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome.” — 1 John 5:3
Jesus said:
“If you love me, you will keep my commandments.” — John 14:15
Christian obedience does not purchase salvation.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works.
But grace does not teach us to become comfortable with sin.
Paul wrote:
“What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means!” — Romans 6:1–2
The Gospel is not:
“Jesus forgives me, therefore nothing needs to change.”
The Gospel announces something infinitely better.
Jesus forgives sinners…
and then begins transforming them.
Maybe that is why your soul has been restless.
You have been asking God to give you peace about something that keeps producing compromise.
But biblical peace is not the same thing as emotional relief.
Sometimes obedience initially hurts.
Sometimes doing the right thing leaves you crying.
Sometimes surrender feels like grief before it feels like freedom.
Remember the rich young ruler.
Jesus looked at him and loved him.
That detail matters.
Christ’s difficult command came from love.
Mark tells us:
“And Jesus, looking at him, loved him…” — Mark 10:21
Then Jesus touched the place the man could not surrender.
The man walked away sorrowful.
Why?
Because he possessed something that, spiritually speaking, possessed him.
Now ask yourself something you may not want to answer.
If Jesus put His finger on this relationship and said:
“Give this to Me.”
Would you?
Or would you walk away sorrowful?
There are relationships where Scripture gives Christians especially serious reasons to stop pretending everything is spiritually neutral.
Paul writes:
The Greek expression begins:
Μὴ γίνεσθε ἑτεροζυγοῦντες ἀπίστοις
Mē ginesthe heterozygountes apistois.
The unusual word heterozygeō evokes being mismatched or unequally joined.
The immediate context is broader than a dating manual; Paul contrasts righteousness with lawlessness, light with darkness, and allegiance to Christ with incompatible spiritual partnership.
So this verse should not be carelessly ripped from context.
Yet its principle matters profoundly when Christians consider intimate covenant-forming relationships.
If Jesus is the center of your existence, choosing someone who fundamentally rejects His lordship is not a small difference of preference.
It reaches into worship.
Marriage.
Children.
Sexual ethics.
Money.
Church.
Prayer.
Suffering.
Purpose.
Death.
Eternity.
Everything.
And Scripture is explicit regarding Christian marriage:
A believer is to marry “only in the Lord.” — 1 Corinthians 7:39.

This does not mean that someone who becomes a Christian while already married to an unbeliever should automatically divorce them. Paul specifically addresses that situation in 1 Corinthians 7:12–16 and tells believers not simply to abandon a willing unbelieving spouse.
Context matters.
Truth matters.
We should never weaponize isolated verses.
But neither should we soften Scripture because obedience is painful.
Maybe your situation is not about an unbelieving partner.
Maybe both of you call yourselves Christians.
But every time you are together, boundaries collapse.
You repent.
Then repeat.
Repent.
Repeat.
Eventually, you stop calling it sin because the word makes you uncomfortable.
Scripture does not tell believers to manage sexual immorality more efficiently.
It says:
φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee from sexual immorality.” — 1 Corinthians 6:18
Pheugete means flee.
Run.
Get away.
Paul does not say flirt with the edge and demonstrate your spiritual maturity by seeing how close you can stand to temptation.
Flee.
Why?
Because God hates you?
No.
Because your body matters to Him.
Because immediately around this command, Paul reminds believers that their bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit and that they were bought with a price.
“Therefore glorify God in your body.” — 1 Corinthians 6:20
There it is.
Glorify God.
Not impress religious people.
Not manufacture shame.
Glorify God.
Jesus paid too high a price for you to casually hand your body, conscience, and worship back to chains He died to break.
But here is where things become deeply personal.
Sometimes you already know.
You know this relationship keeps dragging you backward.
You know you are hiding things.
You know your prayer life has changed.
You know you avoid certain Scriptures because they make the compromise harder to justify.
You know you would be embarrassed if mature believers you respect knew everything happening behind closed doors.
You know the relationship is producing secrecy, rationalization, repeated disobedience, manipulation, or distance from Christ.
Yet you stay.
Why?
Sometimes the answer is not love.
Sometimes it is fear.
Fear that nobody else will choose you.
Fear that you are getting older.
Fear that you already gave them too much.
Fear that starting over means admitting you were wrong.
Fear that the years were wasted.
Fear of seeing them with somebody else.
Fear of sleeping alone.
Fear that surrendering this relationship means surrendering your only chance at happiness.
And underneath all those fears may be one question you have barely dared to say aloud:
“If I give this person to God… will God still take care of my heart?”
That is the real battle.
Trust.
Do you trust Jesus only when He gives?
Or do you trust Him when obedience requires letting go?
Proverbs says:
“Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding.” — Proverbs 3:5
In Hebrew:
בְּטַח אֶל־יְהוָה בְּכָל־לִבֶּךָ
Bəṭaḥ el-YHWH bəḵol-libbekha.
Trust in the LORD with all your heart.
Not the part that understands.
Not the part that feels safe.
Not the part that gets the ending explained beforehand.
All your heart.
And perhaps your heart is breaking even while reading this.
Then hear this carefully:
Jesus is not standing over your brokenness with disgust.
He is not waiting for you to clean yourself up enough to approach Him.
The same Savior who says, “Repent,” is the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
The same Christ who exposes darkness walked toward the cross to rescue people trapped inside it.
Christian conviction is not supposed to end in despair.
It is supposed to lead us home.
Look at Peter.
He swore loyalty to Jesus.
Then denied Him.
Not once.
Three times.
And when the rooster crowed, Peter broke.
Scripture says:
“And he went out and wept bitterly.” — Luke 22:62
Imagine that night.
The shame.
The replaying of his own words.
The sickening realization:
“I said I would never do this.”
Maybe you know that sentence.
“I said I would never go back.”
“I promised God it was over.”
“I knew better.”
“I failed again.”
Peter knew the sound of his own failure.
But failure was not the final chapter.
After the resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
Not to pretend the denial never happened.
Not to call sin acceptable.
Jesus confronted Peter at the level of love:
“Do you love me?” — John 21:15–17
And then restored him to purpose.
“Feed my sheep.”
That is Jesus.
He does not redeem you by convincing you that your sin never mattered.
He redeems you because His grace is greater than your sin.
The cross proves both realities at once.
Sin is so serious that Christ died.
Grace is so astonishing that Christ willingly died for sinners.
This is why the Gospel Warrior theme is not:
“From scandal to pretending nothing happened.”
It is:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Your compromise does not have to become your identity.
Your bad decision does not have to become your permanent address.
The relationship you should never have entered does not have to dictate the rest of your life.
The nights you regret do not outrank the blood of Christ.
Your sexual past does not disqualify you from redemption.
Your emotional dependency is not stronger than the Holy Spirit.
Your shame does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
Paul described believers who had once lived in serious sin and then wrote three breathtaking words:
“And such were some of you.” — 1 Corinthians 6:11
Such were.
Past tense.
Then:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
This is Christianity.
Not people with spotless histories pretending they never fell apart.
Redeemed people standing beneath a bloodstained cross saying:
Jesus saved me.
Jesus washed me.
Jesus is changing me.
Jesus is still writing.
So what do you do if this article has exposed the relationship you have been protecting?
Do not make a reckless decision because an emotional article made you cry.
Go to Scripture.
Pray honestly.
Seek wise, mature Christian counsel from people who care more about your holiness than keeping you comfortable.
Stop hiding the facts that would change their advice.
Look at the fruit.
Is the relationship built upon truth?
Does it honor Christ?
Does it repeatedly require sexual compromise?
Is there manipulation, coercion, deception, abuse, contempt, control, or isolation?
Are you being pulled toward Jesus or slowly trained to put Him second?
And then have the courage to obey what Scripture actually requires.
Not what loneliness wants Scripture to say.
Not what chemistry wants Scripture to say.
Not what social media wants Scripture to say.
What God has said.
If repentance means ending an ungodly dating relationship, then do not call continued compromise “waiting for confirmation.”
If repentance means establishing serious boundaries, establish them.
If repentance means confessing hidden sin, bring it into the light.

If you are married, do not casually apply dating advice to a covenant Scripture treats differently. Seek sound pastoral counsel, especially where betrayal, abuse, abandonment, or serious danger is involved.
But whatever your circumstances…
Do not keep choosing darkness merely because darkness learned your favorite love language.
That sentence may hurt.
You may need it on the night when loneliness starts rewriting history and convincing you that bondage was beautiful simply because it was familiar.
Not to humiliate them.
Not as a passive-aggressive weapon.
Someone scrolling at 1:17 in the morning may be begging God for an answer they are afraid to hear.
Your comment may become someone else’s courage to finally tell the truth.
And please understand something about supporting Gospel Warrior.
If this ministry is helping bring people back to Scripture, back to repentance, back to the cross, and ultimately back to Jesus, supporting it is not about making Gospel Warrior important.
Jesus must remain important.
The Gospel must remain central.
Salvation cannot be bought. God’s grace is not merchandise.

But Christians can glorify God through generous, willing support of faithful Gospel work when that support flows from worship rather than pressure. Scripture teaches that our giving should be voluntary rather than coerced: “not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
They are helping carry a message.
But there is something even bigger than a discount.
Stay close because you want to grow.
Read.
Study.
Wrestle with Scripture.
Grow.
Share what helps you.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who stopped attending church.
Invite the believer who is barely holding on.
Invite the lukewarm Christian who needs awakening.
Invite the seeker who still has questions.
Even invite the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing left to say to them.
and needs to discover that Jesus still restores people.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because somebody you know may be hiding.
Somebody may be praying.
Somebody may be trapped in a relationship they are terrified to surrender.
Somebody may think their scandal has already written the ending.
Let your share interrupt that lie.
Let your comment become a testimony.
Let your tag become an invitation.
Let your support help truth travel farther.
And if this is your story…
come back to Jesus.
Not tomorrow.
Not after one final conversation that becomes another compromise.
Not after you become worthy.
Come with the mess.
Come with the attachment.
Come with the tears.
Come with the screenshots you wish never existed.
Come with the promises you broke.
Come with the parts of the story you are ashamed to tell anybody.
Repentance does not mean pretending you never loved them.
Sometimes repentance means admitting:
“I loved this more than I loved obeying You.”
And grace means discovering that Jesus already knew how deep the attachment went when He called your name.
He knew Peter would deny Him.
He still went to the cross.
He knew your history.
He still went to the cross.
He knew your secret.
He still went to the cross.
He knew every time you would run.
And He still opened His arms.
So perhaps tonight your prayer does not need to be complicated.
“Jesus, I have been holding something tighter than I have been holding You.
Forgive me.
If this relationship is leading me into disobedience, give me courage to stop defending what You are asking me to surrender.
Give me wisdom where the answer is not simple.
Give me godly counsel.
Protect me from confusing loneliness with love, chemistry with covenant, and desire with Your will.
Wash me.
Restore me.
Teach me to love You above everyone and everything.
I surrender what I cannot control.
I surrender the future I imagined.
I surrender the person I am afraid to lose.
And I trust the hands that were pierced for me.
In Jesus’ name.
Amen.”
Maybe you will cry after that prayer.
Maybe tomorrow will still hurt.
Maybe your phone will feel unbearably quiet.
Maybe you will reach instinctively for the person you surrendered.
That does not necessarily mean you made the wrong decision.
Grief can exist beside obedience.
Pain can exist beside freedom.
And surrender can hurt while healing has already begun.
Just remember this when you are tempted to run back:
The hands asking you to surrender are the same hands that were nailed to a cross to save you.
You can trust those hands.
And one day, when you look back at the chapter you thought would destroy you, you may finally understand:
You were terrified Jesus was taking away your whole story… while Jesus was rescuing you from mistaking one painful chapter for the ending.
